alt: The exploding gradient problem: gradients become extremely large during backpropagation, giving huge weight updates and an unstable network. Gradients at the layers are 2 at the output layer, 8, 40 and 200 at hidden layer 1. The fruit example shows predictions of 220 g, 350 g, 80 g, 500 g and 120 g, and a flow ending in unstable learning.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How to solve exploding gradients: gradient clipping (a maximum limit for the gradient), proper weight initialization (He, Xavier), smaller learning rate, batch normalization, and better optimizers (RMSProp, Adam), each with a small picture.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Flow diagram: input x goes to the model with weights W, to output y, to loss L (the forward pass). Backpropagation computes the gradient dL/dW, which the optimizer (GD, Adam, SGD) uses to update the weights: W new equals W old minus eta times dL/dW.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Five steps of how a multilayer feedforward network works for a fruit: input features are given (color red, shape round, weight 180 g, texture smooth), the input layer sends data to hidden layer 1, hidden layer 1 sends information to hidden layer 2, hidden layer 2 learns more complex patterns, and the output layer predicts Apple.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: New concept: a gradient is the slope of the loss function. It tells which direction reduces the loss and how quickly the loss changes, and acts like a guide for the optimizer. A U-shaped loss curve shows a positive gradient (slope above 0) on one side, a negative gradient on the other, and gradient 0 at the minimum point.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Types of gradient: a positive gradient (loss increases as the weight increases, so move the weights in the opposite direction), a negative gradient (loss decreases in the current direction, so continue updating in that direction) and a zero gradient (no slope, updates become very small or stop, near a global minimum, local minimum or saddle point).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How the gradient solves the problem: it is calculated during backpropagation and tells the optimizer to move opposite when it is positive, opposite when it is negative, and that the model may have reached a minimum or saddle point when it is zero. A fruit example shows the prediction moving 220, 205, 193, 182, 180 grams as the loss decreases.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Structure of a multilayer feedforward neural network with an input layer, hidden layer 1, hidden layer 2 and an output layer, with data flow from input to output, and the components: input layer, hidden layer, output layer, neuron, weight, bias and activation function (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, softmax).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Why the loss function cannot solve the problem (it only tells how much error exists, not which weight is wrong, how to update the weights or how to reach the minimum loss) and the new concept: optimization is the process of finding the best values of weights and biases so that the loss becomes as small as possible, using an optimizer.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Quick flow diagram: training data, forward propagation, prediction, loss function, backpropagation, optimizer, update weights, better prediction, which loops back to the training data.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A vertical flow: prediction, loss, backpropagation, gradient (slope), optimizer (uses gradient), update weights, with an arrow back to prediction.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A table of vanishing gradient versus exploding gradient on what happens, weight updates, effect on loss, training behavior, main causes and solutions. Vanishing is solved by ReLU, Leaky ReLU, batch normalization, proper initialization and LSTM/GRU; exploding by gradient clipping, proper initialization, lower learning rate, LSTM/GRU.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The vanishing gradient problem: gradients become extremely small during backpropagation, so earlier layers receive almost no updates and stop learning. Gradients at the layers are 0.8 at the output layer, 0.3, 0.05 and 0.001 at hidden layer 1, so the first hidden layers receive almost zero gradient.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Why vanishing gradients happen: sigmoid outputs values between 0 and 1 and its derivative is always less than 1 (0 less than f'(z) at most 0.25); tanh is zero-centered but its derivative is also at most 1. Many small derivatives are multiplied together, so the gradient becomes almost zero.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How to solve vanishing gradients: ReLU activation (derivative 1 for positive inputs), Leaky ReLU (small gradient for negative inputs), proper weight initialization (He for ReLU, Xavier for sigmoid and tanh), batch normalization (keeps activations in a healthy range) and LSTM or GRU for recurrent networks.
author: Deep Learning faculty
